CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q3 Executive Summary 2 ##### Other precious metal markets ###### Gold The gold market is expected to remain in fundamental surplus over the next five years. After peaking in 2013, the surplus may then decline during the 2014-17 period. - The world’s gold supplies were largely unchanged in the first half of 2012 as a marginal rise in primary gold supply was largely offset by the fall in supply generated by gold recycling programmes. - Central banks continue to diversify their foreign exchange reserves into gold but their interest has started to wane. - Fabrication demand, jewellery in particular, remains weak but is set to improve in later years on the back of lower prices and rising incomes in many key developing countries. ###### Platinum The platinum market surplus is shrinking fast as troubles with supply deepen. The return to a nearly balanced market is now expected in 2014 but it is unlikely that the fundamental balance will shift into deficit at any point in our forecast period. - The decline in platinum mine production is expected to continue in 2013 based in part on the decisions made in 2012 to curtail or defer expansion plans. - Demand from global car manufacturers is expected to strengthen next year thanks to the introduction of Euro VI emissions rules for new vehicles coming into effect on January 1st 2013. - During 2014-17, both supply and demand are likely to grow at approximately the same rate, driven by the new mining projects coming on stream and improved demand on the back of recovering global economy. This should prevent the market from switching into deficit. ###### Palladium Following a significant surplus posted in 2011, the palladium market is set to move into fundamental deficit this year. Fabrication demand ###### 2.1 Summary After bouncing back by 10.4% (or 3,130 tonnes) to 26,940 tonnes in 2010 following the 10.4% drop resulting from the Global Financial Crisis, global fabrication demand is estimated to have slipped by 1.2% (or 320 tonnes). Photographic offtake may have fallen by its smallest absolute rate since 2001 as a result of the saturation of digital technology in the basic consumer photography market, but industrial demand went back into reverse again as well. Demand in 2011 would have fallen much further if silver’s use in coins and medals had not jumped by a further 19.1%. Indeed, excluding coinage, it fell by 3.8% (or 910 tonnes) to 22,940 tonnes. We have global fabrication slipping a little further in 2012. Industrial demand has weakened again as a result of an economic slowdown extending to all regions of the world, but we expect photographic offtake to slip even more slowly and silver’s use in jewellery to just about hold up. However, although we have all this slipping by just 0.7% (or about 150 tonnes), we also have total fabrication contracting by 0.7% (or about 200 tonnes) because we have not seen any further growth in coinage. Nevertheless, coinage still accounts for 14% of all fabrication. Silver’s use in coinage is unlikely to remain elevated when the economy finally recovers and investor interest wanes. However, this will coincide with strong growth in industrial demand, and electronics offtake in particular. Photographic offtake may still be in decline but losses will be modest and we therefore still have the total fabrication rising by 3,275 tonnes in 2012-17 to 29,700 tonnes. This is over 2,000 tonnes higher than the peak in 2000 of 27,640 tonnes. ###### **Coinage will eventually give way to other uses as the main driver of all silver fabrication world fabrication demand; '000 tonnes silver** Others

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q3 Silver 9 ###### 2.2 Jewell

ery & Silverware 

Demand for silver for use in jewellery and silverware decreased by 4.5% (or 300 tonnes) to 6,420 tonnes in 2011.  Having increased by 1.8% (or 120 tonnes) between 2008 and 2010, it has therefore more than offset all of its post-Global Financial Crisis gains.  Moreover, offtake in 2011 was at its lowest level since 1991 when it totalled just 5,960 tonnes, and it was 26.4% (or 2,300 tonnes) below its peak in 2001 when the world economy was in the midst of an economic slowdown.  World GDP in 2001 grew by just 1.4%, a rate which was matched in 2008.  There is clearly no strong link merely between this area of demand and wider economic conditions. 

Silver’s use in jewellery and silverware is largely its most price-elastic area of fabrication demand.  This stems from two main drivers, plus a third lesser influence that have been in action.  To those buyers that consider jewellery and silverware to be discretionary items, silver’s price and the fortunes of the wider economy will have an impact on their willingness to buy.  Of course, fabrication costs must be considered too, and these can be considerable relative to the price of silver.  However, all other things being equal, price will be an increasingly important driver as it rises.  Meanwhile, a squeeze on households’ incomes, or at least the fear of this, has an influence on their ability or willingness to buy silver jewellery and silverware. 

The increase in silver’s price from 2004 has had a clear impact on its use in jewellery and silverware through to 2008.  Italy has historically been at the centre of this activity in Europe, and a gradual rising price has correlated with a steady decline in European jewellery offtake. However, by far the greatest losses during this period were experienced in India where many purchases of silver jewellery and silverware act as a store of wealth alongside gold.  There is evidence that Indian offtake is influenced by the relative prices of silver and gold, with demand for silver losing out when its price strengthens relative to gold as it did in 2004-08.  On the other hand, as agricultural incomes rise in India, gold become increasingly affordable. 

A combination of silver’s price pushing even higher and the spreading of renewed economic weakness has been weighing heavily on silver’s use in jewellery and silverware in 2011-12. Prices are 50-60% higher than their average in 2010 and no region is immune to at least some economic anxieties.  Europe is in the vanguard in respect to deteriorating economic conditions with its GDP having failed to fully recover to its level in 2008 before slipping once again in 2012.  Italy’s silver jewellery market has suffered significantly and this has resulted in Europe’s offtake falling by 19% (or 310 tonnes) to 1,340 tonnes in 2011.  We have it coming off by another 10% (or 130 tonnes) in 2012 so that it stands at just 43% of its peak level in 2000. 

Going forward we expect silver’s use in jewellery and silv

erware to continue to be guided by its price as well as wider economic fortunes. European GDP is only forecast to fully recover all of what it has lost since the Global Financial Crisis in 2014. Growth in global GDP is forecast to re-accelerate through 2013-14 but demand for silver jewellery and silverware is unlikely to recover much just yet if silver’s price is still at about $30/oz. China will be the key driver at this time and, so long as demand elsewhere does not deteriorate much further, we believe that the global total will manage to fully recover its losses since 2010 and total 7,000-7,100 tonnes in 2015. Of course, this still leaves the total 19% (or about 1,650 tonnes) below its high in 2001. However, so long as silver’s price then retreats towards $15/t in 2016-17, we have demand bouncing back to almost 7,800 tonnes in 2017. Silver would then lose out even if gold becomes relatively stronger. ###### 2.3 Photography Silver’s use in photography fell for the twelfth consecutive year in 2011, declining by 7.3% (or 160 tonnes) to 2,040 tonnes. Offtake therefore stood at just 29% of, or 5,060 tonnes below, its peak in 1999 of 7,100 tonnes. The extent of the decline in silver’s use in photography is also notable. A 7.3% decrease is the smallest drop since 2004 when offtake still stood at 79% of its peak in 1999. Moreover, the absolute fall of 160 tonnes in 2011 was the smallest since 2001 which was just the second year of decline in silver’s use in this sector. The sharp slowdown in the erosion of photographic offtake was expected although the precise timing of this transition has been difficult to predict. A number of factors have contributed to this development. The primary driver behind the significant decline in photographic offtake in the 2000s and more recent easing in the rate of contraction is basic photography. Demand fell rapidly as the result of the adoption of digital technology and a point was always going to be approached when it saturated the basic photography market. It was never going to fall below zero, and there are amateur users that are not a

dopting digital technology and these are beginning to support some residual demand for consumer film. This phenomenon helps to explain why the rate of fall in photographic demand slowed substantially in 2011. We would not even rule out the possibility of silver’s use in basic photography beginning to recover. There is evidence of this in Japan. Furthermore, the printing of traditional photographs is still quite a popular choice among digital photographers and so demand for photographic paper may hold up better. While there is the distinct possibility that silver’s use in basic photography could eventually turn, the medical sector will continue to be a source of fabrication losses. However, we doubt that this trend will be rapid, particularly in the short term. The trend between silver demand and the strength of the economy is not always positive. Today’s austerity measures will be cutting investment budgets and, to this end, the take up of digital radiography equipment will surely slow. The rate at which silver’s use in all photographic applications declines should therefore remain moderate at just 3-3.5% through to 2017. This will leave overall photographic offtake at 1,660 tonnes in 2017, a level that is 77% (or 5,440 tonnes) below its peak in 1999. ###### 2.4 Electrical & Electronics Demand for silver for use in electronics has been vital for supporting overall fabrication and is forecast to play a crucial role in future. Electronics offtake is now estimated to have bounced by 35% in 2010 following the 18% fall resulting from the Global Financial Crisis in 2009. The aggressive restocking along the supply chain in 2010 has nevertheless given way, and silver’s use in electrical and electronics items is estimated to have contracted by 3.2% (or 250 tonnes) to 7,470 tonnes in 2011, primarily as a result of disruption to Japanese manufacturing. Our analysis focuses on miners’ pro-rata costs.  Although many miners prefer to report their net of by-product costs, we believe that pro-rata costing is a more useful tool for our analysis. We have looked at the costs of 141 mines in 2011 and these had a combined output of almost 16,000 tonnes (65% of the global total).  Of these mines, 86 had negative net of by-product costs. Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q3 Silver 42 ###### 5.2 Assumed price developments The future level of investor demand, whether in terms of a financial flow or an absolu

te tonnage, will most likely determine silver’s price during the next five years. High prices will be dependent on this latent demand exceeding the fundamental surplus. This scenario could conceivably be broken as this fundamental surplus is fed as a result of high prices encouraging more mine project development and leading to the loss of fabrication demand. However, project funding is far from forthcoming and there is only limited price elasticity of demand. Much of investors’ interest in silver stems from their need for a safe haven and, despite efforts to restore confidence in the global economy, they still believe that there is a high degree of uncertainty. US confirmation of a third round of quantitative easing pushed all metal prices higher but gold and silver have rallied by most with the gold/silver price ratio actually slipping back towards 50. We believe that investor demand for silver will be sustained for so long as interest rates remain low. Three months ago, US interest rates were forecast to rise from 0.4% in 2014 to 1.7% in 2015 and to 3.7% in 2016. They are now forecast to increase to only 0.8% in 2015 and to just 1.6% in 2016. We therefore now have silver’s price holding up through 2015. Our forecast assumes that silver will hold up throughout 2013-14, rising and falling with the ebb and flow of short-term confidence in the global economy and averaging $31/oz in today’s US dollar terms. However, as more robust confidence is restored and monetary policy begins to tighten, we forecast silver’s price falling sharply by the end of 2015. We expect this eventual withdrawal by investors to undermine silver more swiftly than gold. The gold/silver price ratio has previously increased swiftly from 50 to 80-90 and we have such a swing and a decline in gold’s price pushing silver down towards $15/oz in 2016-17. ###### Central banks and investors continue to accumulate gold 

Whilst major central banks have been warming up their “printing presses”, their colleagues, predominantly in emerging markets, have been increasing their gold holdings to diversify away from the USD and the EUR and as an overall strategy of portfolio diversification. 

According to the IMF, net official sector purchases of gold amounted to slightly over 106 tonnes during the first six months of 2012.  Although positive, this volume is 42% lower than a year earlier. 

Central banks of the Philippines and Russia were the most active buyers during the period. Their respective purchases totalled 35.3 tonnes and 35.1 tonnes.  Smaller amounts were purchased by Kazakhstan (19.5 tonnes), Mexico (19.3), Belarus (5 tonnes) and Ukraine (4.8 tonnes). 

Fairly speaking, the 48.9 tonnes increase in gold holdings of the Turkish central bank over the same period, as reported by the IMF, was by far the largest half-year increment in absolute terms.  However, these additions to this bank’s balance sheet are a result of a new policy which allows commerc

ial banks to pledge gold as part of their reserve requirements to the central bank. Since this gold is a form of bank deposit, rather than acquisition by the central bank in the open market, we do not include it in our data. Details of central bank buying interest continued to circulate around the market during July and August. For instance, South Korea’s central bank announced in August that it had bought 16 tonnes of gold in July. We will report on these changes in our next issue after they have been reflected in official statistics releases. Meanwhile, cumulative sales of only 5.1 tonnes of gold were reported by central banks under the third year of Third Central Bank Gold Agreement which runs through the end of September. Although there has been speculation that some eurozone banks might be driven to sell gold to help address the Euro situation, we see no sign of this happening. Bank of International Settlements was amongst the other few sellers of gold. In its annual report for fiscal 2011-12 the bank disclosed information on the sale of 3 tonnes of gold, ipso facto bringing down its total holdings to 116 tonnes. So on the surface it may seem like the Federal Reserve has been pumping extra money directly into the economy. But they have remained low, and overall price increases have remained within the Federal Reserve’s 2% per annum target range. To keep inflation in check the Federal Reserve began developing an exit strategy well before the large-scale asset purchase programmes (QEs) were fully implemented. Despite the positive progress at Lonmin, the situation in South African platinum mining industry is far from over.  In our view, a hefty wage increase the AMCU managed to negotiate with Lonmin has set up a new benchmark and may now trigger a rash of pay demands across the industry forcing other mining companies to play catch up as mineworkers demand equivalent or similar wage improvements to those agreed with Lonmin.  It is illustrative that just within hours after Lonmin deal, mineworkers at neighbouring Anglo American Platinum operations demanded similar hikes and clashed with the police, suggesting more trouble is to come. Recent events appear to be a continuation of the dispute between the NUM and the AMCU which began to heat up in late 2011. 

The NUM is a dominant and a long established union in the South African mining industry with 300,000 members and official recognition at most mines.  The union is affiliated with the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), which is itself affiliated to South Africa’s governing

With the NUM focusing on this year’s ANC elections which are taking place in December, it seems to be unable to respond quickly to worker concerns, so further gains by the AMCU can be expected in the future. ##### Central banks on the offensive 

Recent weeks have seen the world’s major central banks launch action to revive the global economy.  On September 6, the European Central Bank outlined a new bond-buying program, letting markets know that there were no pre-set limits to its purchases.  On September 13, the United States Federal Reserve announced that in the coming months it would purchase some $85 billion of long-term securities per month, with the aim of putting downward pressure on long-term interest rates and supporting growth.  Finally, on September 19, the Bank of Japan declared that it was adding another ¥10 trillion ($128 billion) to its government securities purchase program, and that it expected its total holdings of such paper to reach about $1 trillion by end-2013. 

- At its mid September meeting, the Federal Reserve announced an open-ended programme of quantitative easing (QE3) focused on mortgage-backed securities (MBS) purchases and extended its conditional commitment to leave its policy rate at near-zero until mid-2015. There were numerous other tweaks to its communications strategy, most of which involved shifting the focus of policy away from fixed calendar dates and stressing more that future policy action will depend on how economic conditions develop.  The Fed pledged to make $40bn of MBS purchases per month (plus $45bn worth of purchases as part of its ongoing “operation twist”) and to continue those purchases until it judges that the outlook for the labour market has improved substantially.  Overall, we are doubtful about the impact of QE3 on the real economy, and expect the Fed to increase its purchases sometime in 2013, perhaps re-focusing on treasuries. 

- At its July meeting, the European Central Bank (ECB) cut its main interest rate to a historic low of 0.75% from 1% in mid-July amid signs that prospects for the Eurozone economy are looking increasingly bleak.  Furthermore, at its September meeting it announced a new large scale bond purchase programme aimed at soothing jittery bond markets.  Still, as expected, bond purchases will not be a blank cheque to Eurozone governments.  Conditions will be attached, which the IMF will be asked to set and monitor.   Annual Eurozone inflation accelerated to 2.6% in August from 2.4% in July, coming in stronger than expected and further above the ECB's target of just below 2%. es further as confidence in the region stabilises and inflation remains above target.

##### More exchange rate volatility 

In our forecasts short to medium-term parities are influenced by market-making factors, such as comparative interest rates, which are of a cyclical nature, and inflation expectations, trade deficits and relative growth rates, which are of a more structural nature.  Increasingly, however, some of these structural influences may act in opposition to cyclical influences.  For instance, a currency may not weaken much in response to cuts in interest rates that are made mainly to support growth.  In the long term, however, currencies are projected to revert towards their `fair’ values, which are closely akin to the values implied by purchasing power parities.  In other words currencies are forecast to revert to cross-parities that compensate for the varying prices, in local currency terms, of a common basket of goods.
